{{Short description|Type of cryptanalytic attack}}
In [[cryptography]], '''higher-order differential cryptanalysis''' is a generalization of [[differential cryptanalysis]], an attack used against [[block cipher]]s. While in standard differential cryptanalysis the difference between only two texts is used, higher-order differential cryptanalysis studies the propagation of a set of differences between a larger set of texts. [[Xuejia Lai]], in 1994, laid the groundwork by showing that differentials are a special case of the more general case of higher order derivates.<ref name=lai94>{{cite book | author = [[Xuejia Lai|Lai, Xuejia]] | title = Communications and Cryptography | chapter = Higher Order Derivatives and Differential Cryptanalysis | pages = 227–233 | publisher = Springer US | date = 1994 | volume = 276 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4615-2694-0_23 | isbn = 978-1-4613-6159-6 }}</ref> [[Lars Ramkilde Knudsen|Lars Knudsen]], in the same year, was able to show how the concept of higher order derivatives can be used to mount attacks on block ciphers.<ref name=knudsen94>{{cite conference | author = [[Lars Ramkilde Knudsen|Knudsen, Lars]] | title = Truncated and Higher Order Differentials | conference = [[Fast Software Encryption]] (FSE 1994) | pages = 196–211 | publisher = [[Springer-Verlag]] | date = 1994 | url = http://citeseer.ist.psu.edu/knudsen95truncated.html | format = [[PDF]]/[[PostScript]] | access-date = 2007-02-14 }}</ref> These attacks can be superior to standard differential cryptanalysis. Higher-order differential cryptanalysis has notably been used to break the [[KN-Cipher]], a cipher which had previously been proved to be immune against standard differential cryptanalysis.<ref>{{cite book | author = [[Thomas Jakobsen|Jakobsen, Thomas]] and [[Lars Ramkilde Knudsen|Knudsen, Lars]] | title = Fast Software Encryption | chapter = The interpolation attack on block ciphers | date = 1997 | volume = 1267 | pages = 28–40 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | doi = 10.1007/BFb0052332 | publisher = Springer Berlin Heidelberg | isbn = 978-3-540-63247-4 }}</ref>

==Higher-order derivatives==

A block cipher which maps <math>n</math>-bit strings to <math>n</math>-bit strings can, for a fixed key, be thought of as a function <math>f:\mathbb{F}^n_2\to\mathbb{F}^n_2</math>. In standard differential cryptanalysis, one is interested in finding a pair of an input difference <math>\alpha</math> and an output difference <math>\beta</math> such that two input texts with difference <math>\alpha</math> are likely to result in output texts with a difference <math>\beta</math> i.e., that <math>f(m\oplus\alpha)\oplus f(m) = \beta</math> is true for many <math>m\in\mathbb{F}^n_2</math>. Note that the difference used here is the [[Bitwise XOR|XOR]] which is the usual case, though other definitions of difference are possible.

This motivates defining the derivative of a function <math>f:\mathbb{F}^n_2\to\mathbb{F}^n_2</math> at a point <math>\alpha</math> as<ref name=lai94 />

{{center|<math>\Delta_\alpha f(x) := f(x\oplus\alpha)\oplus f(x)</math>.}}

Using this definition, the <math>i</math>-th derivative at <math>(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_i)</math> can recursively be defined as<ref name=lai94 />

{{center|<math>\Delta^{(i)}_{\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_i} f(x) := \Delta_{\alpha_i}\left(\Delta^{i-1}_{\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_{i-1}}f(x)\right)</math>.}}

Thus for example <math>\Delta^{(2)}_{\alpha_1,\alpha_2} f(x) = f(x)\oplus f(x\oplus\alpha_1)\oplus f(x\oplus\alpha_2)\oplus f(x\oplus\alpha_1\oplus\alpha_2)</math>.

Higher order derivatives as defined here have many properties in common with [[Derivative|ordinary derivative]] such as the [[sum rule in differentiation|sum rule]] and the [[product rule]]. Importantly also, taking the derivative reduces the [[Degree of a polynomial|algebraic degree]] of the function.

==Higher-order differential attacks==

To implement an attack using higher order derivatives, knowledge about the probability distribution of the derivative of the cipher is needed. Calculating or estimating this distribution is generally a hard problem but if the cipher in question is known to have a low [[Degree of a polynomial|algebraic degree]], the fact that derivatives reduce this degree can be used. For example, if a cipher (or the S-box function under analysis) is known to only have an algebraic degree of 8, any 9th order derivative must be 0.

Therefore, it is important for any [[cipher]] or S-box function in specific to have a maximal (or close to maximal) degree to defy this attack.

[[Cube attack]]s have been considered a variant of higher-order differential attacks.<ref name="djb">{{cite web | url = https://cr.yp.to/cubeattacks.html | title = Why haven't cube attacks broken anything? | access-date  = 2014-05-18 | author = [[Daniel J. Bernstein]] | date = 2009-01-14}}</ref>

{{Empty section|date=January 2015}}

==Limitations of Higher-order differential attacks ==

Works for small or low algebraic degree S-boxes or small S-boxes. In addition to AND and XOR operations.
